findings.headline: Enforcement agent follow-up for two NDR debts has stalled for 12+ months with no feedback
findings.detail: Two NDR debts were passed to enforcement agents in July 2025, but there was no feedback from the agents in the previous twelve months on enforcement progress. The council has no visibility into whether these debts are being actively pursued.
findings.matters: Lack of monitoring of outsourced enforcement means the council does not know whether debts are being actively recovered or abandoned. This is a control failure that could result in lost recovery opportunities.
findings.figures: 2 debts with enforcement agents since July 2025; 12+ months without progress update
findings.quote: Two debts had been passed to enforcement agents in July 2025, but there had been no feedback from the agents in the previous twelve months as to how this enforcement was progressing.

findings.headline: NDR debts of £619,401.95 await Cabinet write-off approval, some pending since 2023
findings.detail: Six NDR debts totalling £619,401.95 are awaiting Cabinet approval for write-off with significant delays. One was last actioned in 2025. Two were flagged as waiting in the 2024/25 review. A fourth went into liquidation in 2024 with approval still outstanding. A fifth went bankrupt with approval outstanding from 2023.
findings.matters: Stalled write-off decisions represent unresolved financial positions where the council has determined debts are unrecoverable but has not formally cleared them. Delays suggest procedural breakdown in write-off governance.
findings.figures: £619,401.95 awaiting Cabinet write-off approval; cases pending 1-3 years
findings.quote: Six debts (£619,401.95) were awaiting Cabinet approval for write-off. The last action on one of those was in 2025, whilst two others were flagged as waiting for approval in the 2024/25 review. A fourth case went into liquidation in 2024 with Cabinet approval still outstanding, whilst a fifth case had gone bankrupt, and approval was still outstanding from 2023.

findings.headline: £511.6k in VAT cannot be reclaimed because debts are too old (over 4.5 years)
findings.detail: VAT on sundry debts can only be reclaimed if the debt is between 6 months and 4 years 6 months old. The council has £511.6k in invoices on which VAT cannot be reclaimed due to age.
findings.matters: This represents permanent loss of VAT recovery, reducing net income and increasing the effective cost of unrecovered debts. It signals the council is holding aged, likely irrecoverable invoices.
findings.figures: £511.6k in invoices where VAT cannot be reclaimed
findings.quote: The total amount of invoices for which VAT could not be reclaimed (if applicable) to the debt being over four years and six months old was £511.6k.

findings.headline: £401.9k in debts over 6 years old are time-bound and legally unrecoverable
findings.detail: Cases in legal proceedings worth £401.9k are over six years old and beyond the statutory recovery period. After six years with no correspondence or payment, debts become time-bound and are no longer legally recoverable. The council did not have a spreadsheet to track these cases initially.
findings.matters: Time-bound debts are unrecoverable assets sitting on the books as phantom income. They represent permanent loss and should be written off; their existence overstates collection capacity.
findings.figures: £401.9k in debts over 6 years old; oldest debt invoice raised in 2008
findings.quote: the total value of cases that were being progressed in Legal over six years old totaled £401.9k. In the absence of any spreadsheet monitoring of cases in Legal it was not possible to ascertain if any cases had become time bound

findings.headline: Adult Social Care debt nearly tripled to £22.465m in six years
findings.detail: ASC debt grew from £7.752m (March 2020) to £22.465m (March 2026), with individual resident debts rising from £8.776m to £19.636m. The audit identifies the fundamental issue as delays in Financial Assessments and lack of Accounts Receivable resources. The council is recruiting 5 temporary Debt Recovery Officers on an 18-month spend-to-save basis.
findings.matters: Adult social care debt represents defaults by residents unable or unwilling to pay for care. Rapid growth signals either deteriorating collection effectiveness or increasing service demand without corresponding collection capacity. Council is under-resourced.
findings.quote: the total service debt outstanding was £7.752m. By 31 March 2026 the total debt in connection with the Community Health and Adults Social Care has increased to £22.465m

findings.headline: Total outstanding debt grew 34% in one year, from £73.50m to £98.46m
findings.detail: Outstanding debt jumped from £73.50m (2024/25) to £98.46m (2025/26), a £24.96m increase. Council Tax debt rose from £43.12m to £49.15m. Sundry Debtors nearly doubled from £29.4m to £36.60m, with the number of outstanding invoices growing from 29,134 to 32,805.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing debt indicates either deteriorating collections, rising arrears, or widening service debtor positions. This affects council liquidity and income forecasting.

findings.headline: Audit opinion is Limited Assurance, indicating material control weaknesses in debt recovery
findings.detail: The overall audit opinion across council tax, NNDR and sundry debt systems is Limited Assurance, not Moderate or Substantial. The report identifies multiple gaps: spreadsheets with incomplete data, enforcement agents not monitored for follow-up, Orders for Sale not progressing despite prior-year recommendations, and debts not being written off as approved.
findings.matters: Limited assurance indicates the council's debt management systems are not operating effectively and are not preventing errors or loss. This matters to lenders assessing financial control quality and risk of undetected slippage.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion; 12 recommendations (1 High, 10 Medium, 1 Low priority)
findings.quote: The overall audit opinion is that the controls in place provide Limited assurance.

findings.paper_title: Q4 2025-26 and Q1 2026-27 Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Progress Report
findings.headline: Counter fraud financial outcomes more than doubled in Q1 2026-27 compared to prior quarter
findings.detail: Counter fraud activities identified £220,347.42 in fraud, errors and overpayments in Q1 2026-27, compared to £92,981.48 in Q4 2025-26—a 137% increase. The increase was driven by HB and CTR fraud/error identification spiking from £66,626.05 to £205,306.63.
findings.matters: A material spike in detected fraud could indicate either control weaknesses allowing fraud to go undetected initially, or emerging fraud risk patterns that need investigation.
findings.quote: Total Financial Outcomes from Counter Fraud £92,981.48 £220,347.42

findings.paper_title: Q4 2025-26 and Q1 2026-27 Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Progress Report
findings.headline: Debt Recovery controls remain Limited for second consecutive financial year
findings.detail: The Debt Recovery fundamental financial system (FFS) audit received Limited opinions in both 2024/25 (Q1) and 2025/26 (Q1), indicating control weaknesses have not been resolved. This suggests either initial remediation was ineffective or issues have recurred.
findings.matters: Weak debt recovery controls impair the council's ability to collect cash owed to it, directly affecting liquidity and cash flow forecasting.
findings.figures: Limited opinion in FFS Debt Recovery reviews in consecutive financial years
findings.quote: 2024/25 FFS – Debt Recovery Report Q1 Limited ... 2025/26 FFS - Debt Recovery Report Q1 Limited

findings.headline: System limitations and workarounds: Mosaic upgrades described as ongoing work that 'will not be resolved quickly'
findings.detail: The service cannot currently track foster carer reviews or unannounced visits properly in its Mosaic system and is using manual spreadsheets and interim controls instead. Management states that Mosaic system upgrades are ongoing with IT but will not complete quickly, forcing reliance on weekly manual monitoring and spreadsheets.
findings.matters: Reliance on manual processes and spreadsheets for core financial/operational controls is inherently higher-risk than automated systems. Audit noted the need for system fixes but acknowledged they are not imminent, meaning control weaknesses will persist.
findings.figures: Interim manual controls in place; MOSAIC upgrade timeline unclear but 'not resolved quickly'
findings.quote: The IT service has been approached to facilitate an upgrade of the MOSAIC System which should enable the service to monitor the review process more accurately, and at the time of the review this was ongoing. As an interim measure an additional monitoring field is added to the Foster Carer Register and reviewed weekly by team managers.

findings.headline: No formalized policy for foster care adaptations and extensions; issue unresolved since 2022
findings.detail: At the time of audit (May 2026), the fostering service still had no drafted or formalized policy governing adaptations and extensions for foster carers. The same issue was initially raised in a 2022 briefing note, meaning it has been outstanding for at least four years.
findings.matters: Absence of a policy for capital adaptations creates undefined spending rules and inconsistent decision-making. Foster care adaptations can represent significant capital commitments; without a policy, there is no framework for approving, funding, or limiting such costs.
findings.figures: Policy outstanding since 2022; no guidance at May 2026 audit date
findings.quote: At the time of the review no Adaptions and Extensions Policy had been drafted and formalised. This issue was initially raised in a briefing note in 2022.

findings.headline: A £150 foster care clothing allowance payment recorded in Mosaic with no corresponding client registered in the system
findings.detail: During testing of 15 sundry payments, auditors found one payment of £150 for a clothing allowance that had no corresponding client record in the Mosaic system, indicating either a data integrity failure or an orphaned payment.
findings.matters: Payments without corresponding client records suggest control breakdown in the payment system—funds may be paid without proper authorization or may indicate ghost transactions that mask actual spending.
findings.figures: £150 payment; one of 15 transactions tested
findings.quote: One payment selected related a clothing allowance for £150.00, but there was no record in the Mosaic System of any client for this payment.

findings.headline: Mockingbird scheme carer payments were made at rates higher than agreed, with authorization only added retrospectively in November 2025
findings.detail: Carers in the Mockingbird scheme with enhanced responsibilities received higher rates than standard carers. These non-standard rates were paid first and formal authorization was added afterward in November 2025, rather than being pre-approved.
findings.matters: Retrospective authorization of above-standard payments suggests weak pre-spend approval processes and creates potential for uncontrolled wage inflation or scope creep in service delivery costs.
findings.figures: Mockingbird scheme carers paid above agreed rates; retrospective agreement November 2025
findings.quote: Various payments were made to carers involved in the Mockingbird scheme who had enhance responsibilities and as such were paid higher rates than other carers. The rates paid to these carers were above those agreed for other carers and agreed retrospectively in November 2025.

findings.headline: Carer supervision visit monitoring shows eight visits overdue since October 2025 and 10-carer discrepancy between tracking systems
findings.detail: The service aims to conduct two unannounced visits per carer per year. Monitoring spreadsheets show eight carers with visits overdue since 2025, oldest from 27/10/2025. Additionally, the home visits spreadsheet covers 190 carers while the reviews spreadsheet covers 200, indicating data integrity issues.
findings.matters: Unannounced visits are a statutory minimum standard for carer supervision. Missing visits and tracking discrepancies represent both regulatory risk and control failure that suggest poor operational oversight.
findings.figures: 8 overdue visits; oldest since 27/10/2025; 190 vs 200 carers tracked; 2 visits per carer annually targeted
findings.quote: A total of eight carers were shown to be outstanding from 2025, with the oldest one being outstanding since 27/10/2025. In total the spreadsheet detailed 190 carers where home visits were being monitored, but the spreadsheet maintained detailing foster carer reviews listed 200 carers being monitored.

findings.headline: Only 58% of required foster carer annual reviews completed on time; reviews outstanding from October 2023 remain unactioned
findings.detail: In 2024/25, 83 annual reviews were due but only 58% were completed within agreed timescales. Of the 200 foster carers requiring reviews, one review from October 2023 and another from July 2024 remain outstanding, plus 35 cases from 2025 and 24 cases due as of January 2026 with no action recorded.
findings.matters: Overdue reviews represent a compliance and safeguarding failure that auditors flagged as high-priority, indicating the service lacks basic operational control. For lenders, persistent non-compliance across 42% of a core process suggests deeper management or capacity issues.
findings.figures: 58% on-time completion; 200 carers monitored; reviews outstanding since Oct 2023, July 2024; 35 overdue from 2025; 24 due Jan 2026 unactioned
findings.quote: Of these, one review was still outstanding from 01/10/2023, whilst another was outstanding from 01/07/2024. Thirty-five cases were shown as still being outstanding from 2025, and twenty-four cases were due as at 01/01/2026, none of which appeared to have been actioned.

findings.headline: Payment authorizations previously fell entirely outside the council's Constitution and Scheme of Delegation
findings.detail: Before September 2025, carer managers were approving payments with no formal evidence of delegated authority. The approval levels did not reflect the council's constitutional Scheme of Delegation, and no bespoke scheme had been formally agreed for the fostering service.
findings.matters: Unauthorized approval structures represent a fundamental control failure that could result in improper or wasteful spending without proper oversight, increasing fraud and error risk.
findings.figures: All payments prior to September 2025; carer managers were approvers without documented authority
findings.quote: It was not possible to ascertain where the levels of delegated authority had been agreed allowing the carer's managers to approve payments. The approvals appeared to fall outside the Scheme of Delegation outlined in the Councils Constitution, and no bespoke Scheme of Delegation had been formally agreed.

findings.headline: Nine foster care payments made without documented authorization evidence after new controls were introduced
findings.detail: In September 2025, the council implemented new spending controls requiring director-level approval for fostering payments. However, nine payments made after this date could not be matched with authorization evidence in either the Agresso or Mosaic systems.
findings.matters: Payments without documented authorization are a governance failure that creates audit risk and suggests the new control system is not yet embedded, leaving the service vulnerable to further unauthorized expenditure.
findings.figures: 9 payments post-September 2025; controls require director approval
findings.quote: It was not possible to obtain the relevant authorisations for nine payments made after September 2025 under the new spending control.

findings.headline: Audit opinion downgraded to Limited due to control weaknesses in payments and monitoring
findings.detail: The fostering service received a Limited audit opinion rather than an adequate one. The auditors found multiple material control issues: payment authorizations falling outside the council's Scheme of Delegation, inadequate monitoring of carer supervision visits, and lack of a comprehensive authorization framework.
findings.matters: A Limited audit opinion on a significant council service signals that financial controls are not operating effectively, creating risk of overspending, improper expenditure, or compliance breaches that could affect the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Multiple high-priority findings across foster care payments, reviews, and monitoring
findings.quote: There were several internal control issues which require strengthening. These were around the payment of sundry expenses and the lack of a comprehensive Scheme of Delegation in respect of the amounts of payments and the authorisation of payments.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Report of the Audit Committee to Council
findings.headline: Audit committee did not receive regular reports on corporate risk register, information governance, or local code of governance during 2025/26
findings.detail: The committee identified in its own effectiveness review that it failed to receive regular updates on three key governance elements: the Corporate Risk Register, SIRO (Senior Information Risk Owner) reports, and the Local Code of Corporate Governance. The report explicitly states these gaps and plans to address them in 2026/27, but this represents a year where governance oversight was incomplete.
findings.matters: Gaps in audit committee oversight mean risks and governance issues may not have been properly escalated or managed. For a lender, this suggests governance weaknesses may not be fully visible even to the council's own oversight body.
findings.figures: Local Code of Corporate Governance not reported; Corporate Risk Register not reported regularly; SIRO updates not received
findings.quote: During the 2025/26 The Audit Committee has not received reports on the following elements of the Council's assurance framework: the Local Code of Corporate Governance, the Corporate Risk Register or SIRO update reports.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Report of the Audit Committee to Council
findings.headline: Head of Internal Audit issued Limited Assurance opinion for both 2024/25 and 2025/26, a governance control weakness flagged by external audit
findings.detail: The council's internal audit function gave a Limited Assurance opinion on governance and control arrangements for two consecutive years. While the council established detailed reporting to senior leaders and the committee, the underlying assurance level has not improved. The external auditor specifically flagged this as a significant weakness in governance arrangements.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance from internal audit means the council's system of internal controls is not providing the level of confidence lenders expect. This directly affects the reliability of financial reporting and the council's ability to prevent or detect fraud and error.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion for 2024/25 and 2025/26; expected improvement 'should current momentum be sustained throughout 2026/27'
findings.quote: the overall conclusion and Annual Audit Opinion is that the Council's systems of governance and internal control during 2025/26 continued to provide Limited assurance, there is a clear implementation plan in place and a positive trajectory of improvement

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Report of the Audit Committee to Council
findings.headline: External auditor identified reliance on reserves to support revenue expenditure as a significant financial sustainability weakness
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars' 2024/25 audit identified this as a material value-for-money weakness. The council responded during 2025/26 by increasing earmarked and revenue grant reserves to provide future revenue budget support if needed, but this response confirms the core problem: the council is funding current operations from reserves rather than from sustainable revenue sources.
findings.matters: Reliance on reserves to balance revenue budgets is unsustainable and signals deteriorating financial resilience. Lenders need to know whether a council can fund its operations from current income or whether it is depleting reserves to cover deficits.
findings.figures: Two significant value-for-money weaknesses identified for 2024/25; council increased earmarked reserves and revenue grant reserves during 2025/26
findings.quote: The External Auditor did however note two significant value for money weaknesses in relation to Financial Sustainability (reliance on reserves to support revenue expenditure), and Governance

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Head of Audit Annual Report and Opinion to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Corporate Risk Register has not been reported to Audit Committee during 2025/26; governance oversight gap identified
findings.detail: The council's Corporate Risk Register, which identifies strategic risks to council objectives, was not presented to the Audit Committee during the financial year. Last update was March 2025. Audit identifies this as a fundamental governance gap.
findings.matters: Risk management is core governance requirement; absence of regular reporting to committee indicates oversight failure; lenders rely on councils identifying and managing strategic risks.
findings.figures: No Corporate Risk Register reporting 2025/26; last update March 2025
findings.quote: The Council's Corporate Risk Register was not presented to the Audit Committee during 2025/26. Effective management of risk is a fundamental pillar of good governance.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Head of Audit Annual Report and Opinion to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Newly-acquired care home (Oldham Total Care) assessed at weak governance; improvements still ongoing after two years
findings.detail: Council acquired Oldham Total Care in July 2023 after previous operator (Chadderton Total Care) entered administration. This served ~100 residents with complex nursing needs. Audit review found governance and financial administration arrangements require 'further strengthening' and rates assurance as Weak.
findings.matters: Council owns and operates material service (care home); weak governance on integration indicates risk to residents, staff, and council balance sheet; continued work post-acquisition raises questions about due diligence.
findings.figures: ~100 residents; ~200 staff affected; acquisition July 2023; assurance assessment: Weak
findings.quote: Our review of the governance and financial administration arrangements at Oldham Total Care identified a number of areas where structures, systems and processes would benefit from further strengthening to fully support the effective governance of the organisation. While this work is still ongoing since the Council acquired the business, the current level of assurance is assessed as Weak

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Head of Audit Annual Report and Opinion to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Audit explicitly warns that continued use of reserves to fund revenue overspends threatens council financial resilience in future periods
findings.detail: The audit opinion states that continued patterns of drawing reserves to cover revenue expenditure overspends present a direct risk to the council's financial resilience and ability to manage future financial pressures.
findings.matters: Direct audit warning of unsustainable practice; reduced financial resilience increases credit risk and limits council's ability to respond to shocks or discretionary expenditure.
findings.figures: Council exceeded budget by £3.845m in 2025/26, funded from reserves
findings.quote: However, should the use of reserves to support revenue expenditure continue, the Council risks the prospect of reduced financial resilience in future periods.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Head of Audit Annual Report and Opinion to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Outstanding debt has nearly doubled in six years, rising from £46.99m to £98.46m; progress on collection continues into 2026/27
findings.detail: Council Tax debt rose from £24.53m (2018/19) to £49.15m (2025/26); Non-Domestic Rates from £6.29m to £12.71m; Sundry Debtors from £16.17m to £36.60m. Council is pursuing orders for sale, bankruptcy and winding up petitions but implementation is ongoing into 2026/27 with outcomes anticipated going forward.
findings.matters: Doubling of historic debt represents significant cash flow and credit risk; slow implementation of recovery strategy suggests collection weakening or economic factors affecting council taxpayers.
findings.figures: Total debt 2018/19: £46.99m; 2025/26: £98.46m. Council Tax: £24.53m to £49.15m; NNDR: £6.29m to £12.71m; Sundry Debtors: £16.17m to £36.60m
findings.quote: substantially increased levels of debt across all of these areas, and this trend has continued into 2025/26 as shown in the table below which, in the case of NNDR and Council Tax, shows the debt outstanding at 31st March each year relating to prior years, i.e. historic debt excluding in-year debt.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Head of Audit Annual Report and Opinion to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Council overspent 2025/26 budget by £3.845m and used one-off accounting mechanisms to reduce the apparent position by ~£11m
findings.detail: Unaudited financial results show the council exceeded budget by £3.845m (down from ~£10m in 2024/25). Overspend was funded from reserves plus a 'one-off facility' to capitalize capital project interest charges, reducing reported in-year position by approximately £11m. Council has increased earmarked reserves for future revenue support.
findings.matters: Use of accounting mechanisms to recharacterize revenue costs as capital (interest capitalization) masks underlying spending control problems; reliance on reserves indicates structural deficit.
findings.figures: 2025/26 overspend £3.845m (2024/25 c£10m); one-off interest capitalization facility ~£11m
findings.quote: the Council exceeded its annual budget by £3.845m. (2024/25 c£10m) This overspend was funded from the Council's reserve balances available for this purpose and also a one-off facility available to capitalise capital project interest charges and reduce the 2025/26 in-year overspend position by approximately £11m.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Head of Audit Annual Report and Opinion to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Council systems provide limited assurance for second consecutive year after five years of unresolved control weaknesses
findings.detail: Fundamental financial systems covering Payroll, Direct Payments, Residential Care, Children's Social Care, and Debt Recovery have provided Limited assurance for multiple years despite repeated audit recommendations. Three of these systems cover high-volume council expenditure, particularly adult and children's social care.
findings.matters: Persistent control weaknesses in material spending areas indicate systematic governance failures that are not being remedied; increases risk to service delivery and financial accuracy.
findings.figures: Five fundamental financial systems remain Limited assurance; Payroll, Children's Social Care, and Debt Recovery have been Inadequate/Limited for three consecutive years (2023/24 onwards)
findings.quote: The 2024/25 Annual Opinion Report noted that the Council had made insufficient progress in addressing areas of persistent control weakness in five Fundamental Financial Systems over a number of years. These were Payroll, Direct Payments and Community Homecare, Residential Care Payments, Children's Social Care Payments and Debt Recovery. Payroll and Social Care Payments represent a significant portion of the Council's annual expenditure.

findings.headline: Staffing instability and turnover in audit and governance functions
findings.detail: High staff turnover in the council, particularly in internal audit, is cited as the primary cause of limited assurance ratings and control failures. This suggests capacity and continuity problems in the functions responsible for governance.
findings.matters: Staffing instability undermines governance and financial control capacity. If the council cannot retain people in audit and finance roles, control design and execution both suffer.
findings.figures: High turnover; limited assurance opinions most commonly due to staffing issues
findings.quote: Review of the limited assurance opinions highlights that most have been issued due to issues with staffing and high turnover of staff.

findings.headline: Management failing to implement internal audit recommendations within agreed timeframes
findings.detail: Officers have not been implementing medium and high priority internal audit recommendations within agreed deadlines. High priority recommendations have been outstanding for multiple financial years without completion, indicating a pattern of non-response to identified control deficiencies.
findings.matters: Failure to implement audit recommendations signals weak management accountability and suggests governance risks are not being remedied. Lenders rely on councils responding to audit findings.
findings.figures: High priority recommendations outstanding over multiple years
findings.quote: officers are failing to implement medium and high priority actions within agreed timeframes to address identified deficiencies in internal control, with evidence that high priority recommendations have been reported over a number of financial years.

findings.headline: Internal audit issued limited assurance opinion over governance and controls
findings.detail: The council's Head of Internal Audit gave a limited assurance rating on governance, risk management, and internal control arrangements across the council in 2024/25. Most limited assurance opinions have been driven by staffing problems and high turnover, plus failure to comply with control systems.
findings.matters: Limited assurance indicates systemic control weaknesses across multiple council directorates, not isolated to one area—this suggests pervasive governance risk.
findings.figures: Limited assurance opinion issued; issues affect multiple directorates
findings.quote: The Head of Internal Audit issued a limited assurance opinion over the Council's governance, risk management, and internal control arrangements in place during 2024/25. Review of the limited assurance opinions highlights that most have been issued due to issues with staffing and high turnover of staff. In addition, there is evidence of failure to comply with reasonably designed systems of control.

findings.headline: General fund reserves depleted by 38% to £44.9m
findings.detail: The failure to deliver savings and the overspend directly reduced the council's financial reserves by more than a third in a single year. This reduces financial resilience and the buffer available for unexpected costs or further shortfalls.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion limits the council's financial flexibility and increases refinancing risk if income shortfalls or demand spikes occur.
findings.figures: General fund reserves reduced by 38% to £44.9m
findings.quote: The Council's failure to control levels of expenditure or deliver its savings plans increases the risk of the Council having insufficient reserves to deliver its services.

findings.headline: Missed £20.4m savings target and £10.1m overspend in 2024/25
findings.detail: The council set a balanced budget for 2024/25 requiring £20.4m of savings. By year-end it had overspent by £10.1m and delivered only £15.9m (77%) of planned savings. This is flagged by the external auditor as a significant weakness in financial planning.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver a planned savings programme and control expenditure signals financial management risk to lenders assessing the council's reliability.
findings.figures: £20.4m savings target, £15.9m delivered, £10.1m outturn overspend
findings.quote: The Council failed to deliver its savings requirement in full, with only £15.9m out of the target £20.4m achieved. This has resulted in the Council's earmarked general fund reserves reducing by 38% to £44.9m.

findings.paper_title: Payroll Audit progress report - Audit Committee July 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: Council's own recovery plan is acknowledged to be insufficient; improvements will take longer than the current 12-month plan to develop and embed
findings.detail: The HR & OD ReBuild Recovery Plan launched September 2025 is designed as a 12-month intervention. However, management explicitly acknowledges that improvements will extend beyond this period, and further plans will need to be developed to achieve full remediation.
findings.matters: Extended timelines for remediation mean the council will continue operating with known control weaknesses in a critical service for a prolonged period; this affects confidence in the adequacy of financial controls and management's baseline capability.
findings.figures: 12 months for initial plan; full improvement timeline undefined but acknowledged as longer
findings.quote: It is acknowledged that improvements will take longer than 12 months to develop and embed, so further plans will need to be developed.

findings.paper_title: Payroll Audit progress report - Audit Committee July 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: Payroll service has been classified as 'Inadequate/Limited Assurance' for years and the 25/26 audit still reports Limited Assurance
findings.detail: The payroll service carries long-standing identified issues that have led to multi-year inadequate/limited assurance classifications. The 25/26 audit reported Limited Assurance even as the recovery plan began launching, indicating the weakness persists. The service handles not just Oldham's own payroll but also services schools and external providers.
findings.matters: Payroll controls are fundamental to financial stewardship; weakness in a critical transaction stream indicates broader control environment concerns that affect a lender's assessment of financial governance and management capability.
findings.figures: Multiple years of inadequate/limited assurance; 25/26 audit Limited Assurance
findings.quote: The Payroll service at Oldham Council has several, long-standing identified issues, which has led to it being classified as "Inadequate/Limited Assurance" by Internal Audit for a number of years.

findings.headline: £10m of LOBO loans were called and refinanced at 6.70-7.67%, significantly above the 4.33% portfolio average
findings.detail: During 2025/26, lenders exercised options on £10m of LOBO loans, proposing new rates of 6.70% and 7.67%. The council repaid these loans immediately rather than accept the higher rates. As of 31 March 2026, the council still holds approximately £76m in LOBO loans, with £39m having call dates within the next 12 months, creating ongoing exposure to potentially unfavorable refinancing.
findings.matters: This demonstrates the council incurred material refinancing costs (200+ basis points above the portfolio average) and faces ongoing exposure to higher rates if remaining LOBO lenders exercise their options.
findings.figures: £10m repaid at 6.70% and 7.67% (versus 4.33% average LOBO rate); £76m total LOBO loans remaining; £39m with call dates within 12 months
findings.quote: A Call option for £5m FMS Westmanagement was called on 31st March 2025 with a proposed interest rate of 7.67% and repaid 6/4/2025. A further loan to Dexia was called wit a proposed interest rate of 6.70% and was also repaid 23 December 2025.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee Report - Accounting Policies and Critical Judgements
findings.headline: Council holds £85.5m in LOBO loans with significant embedded interest rate risk
findings.detail: The Council's debt portfolio includes £85.5m of Lender Option Borrower Option (LOBO) loans with overall terms of approximately 50 years. These loans contain interest rate variation clauses at option intervals ranging from 6 months to 5 years. At each option date, the lender has the right to vary the interest rate and the Council can elect to repay the loan or accept the new rate. The Council's accounting treatment assumes that none of the lender options will be called.
findings.matters: This represents material debt exposure with significant interest rate and refinancing risk. If lenders exercise their options during periods of rising interest rates, the Council could face substantial increases in debt service costs, affecting financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £85.5m outstanding LOBO loans with ~50 year overall terms and option intervals of 6 months to 5 years
findings.quote: The Council has £85.5m of outstanding LOBO loans in its debt portfolio which have long overall loan lengths (c 50 years). The Loans have option date frequencies of between 5 years and 6 months. At each option date the lender can choose to vary the interest rate payable on the loans and the Council can choose to repay the loan in full or accept the new interest rate.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Q3 to Audit committee March 2026
findings.headline: Interest rate exposure is growing as planned capital spending increases external borrowing requirements across the forecast period
findings.detail: Capital Financing Requirement is increasing from £559.839m to forecast £586.263m by March 2027, driven by planned capital expenditure of £102.464m in 2026/27. As the council moves from internal borrowing to external debt, sensitivity to interest rate changes grows. Finance costs are forecast to rise from £31.315m to £34.987m. A 1% rise in rates would add £103k initially, escalating to £649k by 2027/28.
findings.matters: Growing interest rate exposure reduces budget certainty and increases vulnerability to monetary policy shocks. A lender assesses whether a council's revenue budget can absorb a sustained increase in borrowing costs.
findings.figures: Financing costs forecast £31.315m (2025/26) rising to £34.987m (2027/28); 1% rate rise impact £103k (2025/26) rising to £649k (2027/28); CFR increasing £9.343m year-on-year
findings.quote: Following advice from external Treasury Advisors we are currently borrowing in smaller values whilst monitoring the interest rates.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Q3 to Audit committee March 2026
findings.headline: Council has provisioned £2m for potential losses on pooled property fund if statutory accounting override expires
findings.detail: The council holds £13.615m in the CCLA pooled property fund, expected to return £0.630m in 2025/26. MHCLG's statutory override exempting councils from recognising unrealised losses expires 1 April 2029. The council has made a £2m revenue provision against the risk that the override is not extended and losses must be recognised in the accounts.
findings.matters: Creates a contingent liability on the revenue budget, dependent on government policy decisions. If realised, would materially impact reserves unless covered from that year's outturn.
findings.figures: £2.000m provision made; £13.615m invested in CCLA property fund; £0.630m forecast annual return; statutory override effective until 1 April 2029
findings.quote: The Authority has provided for a loss of up to £2.000m, to mitigate the impact on the revenue budget of the statutory override not being extended and un-realised losses on pooled investment funds are required to be recognised.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Q3 to Audit committee March 2026
findings.headline: £39m of LOBO loans face call dates within the next 12 months, creating significant refinancing risk outside council control
findings.detail: The council holds £39m of LOBO loans where the lender can force a rate reset: £19m with Dexia Finance, £10m with KBC Bank, and £10m split between Just Retirement and Danske. A £5m Dexia tranche has already been called. If rates remain elevated or rise further, refinancing these maturing tranches will be materially more expensive than current rates (averaging 4.32%).
findings.matters: Refinancing risk is material and largely outside the council's control. A lender needs to assess whether the council has sufficient budget flexibility to absorb step changes in borrowing costs when these loans mature.
findings.figures: £39.000m LOBO loans callable within 12 months; £5m already called by Dexia; £75.500m total LOBO holdings at weighted average rate 4.32%
findings.quote: Currently Oldham Council has £39.000m LOBO loans  with call dates  within the next 12 months.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Q3 to Audit committee March 2026
findings.headline: Reserves depletion will force external borrowing as the council's current self-financing model becomes unsustainable
findings.detail: The council has maintained an under-borrowed position by using cash reserves to fund capital rather than external debt. This strategy is now reaching its limit. As revenue expenditure continues to draw down reserves, the capacity to finance capital this way will disappear, forcing external borrowing at market rates. Internal borrowing has already increased from £101.210m to £117.584m in nine months.
findings.matters: Shift from internally-financed to externally-financed capital increases borrowing costs and reduces budget flexibility. Lenders need visibility of the council's forward borrowing trajectory and capacity to absorb higher debt-service costs.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing increased £16.374m to £117.584m; net borrowing increased from £187.231m to £194.647m; CFR forecast to reach £586.263m by March 2027
findings.quote: However, as the Council utilises its reserves to finance annual revenue expenditure, the capacity to do this will diminish and external borrowing will be required.

findings.headline: Accelerated year-end closedown allows reserve decisions to be made after the fact without prior member scrutiny
findings.detail: The policy permits the Director of Finance to make reserve creation and decommissioning decisions at year-end closure without prior formal reporting to management board or members, with reporting only after accounts close.
findings.matters: Lack of prospective approval and transparency over reserve decisions represents a governance weakness and increases the risk of unscrutinised use of reserves to disguise or defer budget problems.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: In addition, given the accelerated timeline for the closure of the accounts, decisions will need to be taken about the use and creation of reserves without the opportunity to formally report these to Management Board/Members in advance. Key issues arising in relation to reserves in such instances will be determined at the discretion of the Director of Finance and will be reported after the Council's accounts have closed.

findings.headline: Service volatility risk requires £4.220m risk reserve with mandatory replenishment if used
findings.detail: The council identifies a specific requirement for a £4.220m Risk Reserve to provide for service volatility above base budget. Use can only be approved by Chief Executive and Director of Finance, and if drawn, must be replenished as a priority.
findings.matters: The requirement to replenish this reserve as a priority suggests it has been used before and the council anticipates continued need. High service volatility that cannot be managed within budget is a stress indicator.
findings.figures: Risk Reserve: £4.220m (2025-26 opening balance)
findings.quote: It has been identified that a risk reserve at £4.220m is required to provide financial resource for additional service volatility over and above the base budget provision available. Any use of this reserve can only be approved by the Chief Executive and Director of Finance and if used, should be replenished as a priority.

findings.headline: Director of Finance has broad discretion to liquidate any reserve to balance the budget
findings.detail: The policy explicitly grants the Director of Finance authority to decommission any reserve where necessary to support delivery of a balanced budget, with no prior member approval required.
findings.matters: This discretionary authority signals financial stress and the risk that reserves intended for specific purposes may be raided to patch annual budget gaps rather than addressing structural deficits.
findings.figures: Total reserves subject to potential decommissioning: £43.6m
findings.quote: The Director of Finance is able to decommission any reserves where it is deemed necessary to do so to support the Council in delivering a balanced budget.

findings.headline: Schools budget has cumulative multi-year deficit now offset by a finite £3.996m reserve
findings.detail: A DSG Surplus Reserve of £3.996m was created to offset a cumulative DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit held in unusable reserves. This is a one-off accounting mechanism masking a structural problem in schools funding.
findings.matters: When this reserve is exhausted, the deficit becomes a real liability that will need to be addressed. A cumulative multi-year schools deficit indicates systemic underfunding or overspend in the schools portfolio.
findings.figures: DSG Surplus Reserve: £3.996m (end of financial year); Cumulative DSG deficit amount not disclosed
findings.quote: The reserve offsets the cumulative DSG deficit which is held in unusable reserves. The balance held in this reserve at the end of the financial year was £3.996m.

findings.headline: Reserves have declined over several years while revenue budget pressures persist
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it is experiencing a multi-year reduction in reserves combined with continued revenue budget pressures, which prompted a full policy review. This suggests the council's financial cushion is eroding.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown combined with ongoing budget pressure is a key indicator of financial resilience risk for lenders assessing the council's capacity to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: No specific drawdown amounts given; reference is to "several financial years" of reduction
findings.quote: The reduction in reserves over several financial years and the continued pressures on the Council's revenue budget means that there is a need to review the Council's reserves policy to ensure it reflects the organisation's priorities.

findings.paper_title: 4. Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 202627 to 203031
findings.headline: Significant capital borrowing of £58.3m over five years, with £33m in the first year alone
findings.detail: The capital programme is heavily front-loaded, with £102.464m (58.8% of the five-year total) planned for 2026/27, declining sharply to £49.047m, £14.923m, £5.972m and £1.592m in subsequent years. Prudential borrowing of £33.039m (32% of 2026/27 spend) is required to finance this, totalling £58.321m over the five-year programme, on top of existing council debt.
findings.matters: The heavily front-loaded programme and significant borrowing increase the council's debt burden and create delivery risk. A lender needs to understand why the programme is so concentrated in year one and how the sharp subsequent decline will be managed.
findings.quote: The proposed Capital Strategy and programme for 2026/27 to 2030/31 takes the essential elements of the 2025/26 to 2029/30 and previous years' strategies and programmes and moves them forward in the context of the financial and political environment for 2026/27

findings.paper_title: 4. Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 202627 to 203031
findings.headline: Capital programme dependent on asset disposals generating £11.8m capital receipts over 4 years; disposal programme under review
findings.detail: The financing plan requires capital receipts of £3.751m (2026/27), £2.900m (2027/28), £2.600m (2028/29) and £2.600m (2029/30) to fund schemes and support the revenue transformation programme. The council's Medium Term Property Strategy is currently under review as part of the Creating a Better Place programme. If asset sales underperform, a funding gap emerges.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the assumed asset receipt stream is realistic, particularly given that the property strategy is under review and backlog maintenance is competing with disposal objectives.
findings.figures: £11.851m capital receipts assumed over 2026/27-2029/30; current 2025/26 receipts position shows £1.103m surplus but requires £5.817m total
findings.quote: another objective of the property strategy is to reduce the requirement for backlog maintenance and inform the development of an asset disposals programme to reduce Council holdings of surplus assets and generate additional capital receipts

findings.paper_title: 4. Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 202627 to 203031
findings.headline: Supply chain inflation and construction cost risks being mitigated through increased contingency reserve
findings.detail: The council has increased unallocated funding for cost pressures from £3.408m to £5.000m (an increase of £1.592m), specifically to protect against scheme cost overruns from supply chain issues and inflation. This suggests the council is experiencing or anticipating cost increases on existing schemes.
findings.matters: Rising construction costs could impact overall affordability and deliverability of the capital programme, potentially requiring further borrowing or deferral of lower-priority schemes.
findings.figures: Reserve increased by £1.592m; total contingency now £5.000m over 5-year period
findings.quote: The Capital Strategy also includes an additional unallocated resource to mitigate against the risk of scheme cost increases resulting from supply chain issues in the construction sector and associated inflationary pressures

findings.paper_title: 4. Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 202627 to 203031
findings.headline: Nearly half of 2026/27 capital programme funded by government grants not yet allocated
findings.detail: The council has not received all grant allocations for 2026/27. Ringfenced and un-ringfenced grants totalling £62.577m (61% of the £102.464m planned expenditure) are based on forecasts and expected allocations. If allocations are lower than projected, the shortfall will need to be funded from prudential borrowing or by deferring schemes.
findings.matters: Significant uncertainty about funding availability in year one creates risk of either programme deferral or unplanned additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £49.882m ringfenced grants + £12.695m un-ringfenced grants = £62.577m of £102.464m total (2026/27)
findings.quote: The Council has not yet received all the grant allocations for 2026/27, and any new funding will be incorporated into future updates

findings.paper_title: 4. Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 202627 to 203031
findings.headline: Revenue budget dependent on £2.6m annual capital receipts funding that expires in 2030, creating a cliff
findings.detail: The Council is using flexible capital receipt powers to fund £2.6m of transformation expenditure from the revenue budget each year through 2030. This policy direction expires in 2030, leaving a £2.6m annual shortfall in revenue funding after that date unless alternative sources are secured. The strategy does not outline how this will be replaced.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how the council will fund its ongoing transformation activities post-2030, and whether further borrowing or service cuts will be necessary.
findings.figures: £2.600m annually 2026/27-2030/31; expiry date 2030
findings.quote: The 2026/27-2030/31 revenue budget will rely on up to £2.600m of funding from capital receipts each year until the expiry of the capital direction in 2030

findings.headline: £34m of LOBO loans face refinancing options in 2026-27; rising interest rates increase probability lenders will exercise options to increase rates
findings.detail: The council holds £75.5m of LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans. Of these, £34m have contractual option dates in 2026-27 when lenders can propose rate increases. The paper explicitly notes that with long-term interest rates having risen in recent years, lenders are likely to exercise these options. The council's policy is to repay rather than accept higher rates, meaning unexpected refinancing and cash flow impact.
findings.matters: LOBO loans create uncontrolled refinancing risk: the council cannot predict the timing or cost of debt service increases beyond its control, and forced repayment of £34m alongside new borrowing needs of £36.8m creates refinancing pressure in a single financial year.
findings.figures: £75.5m total LOBO loans outstanding; £34m have options during 2026-27
findings.quote: £34m of these LOBOs have options during 2026/27, and with long term interest rates having risen in recent years, lenders may seek to exercise their options. If they do, the Council will look to take the option to repay LOBO loans to reduce refinancing risk in later years.

findings.headline: Council transitioning from cash reserves to external borrowing: forecast to require £36.8m new borrowing in 2026-27 after years of holding surplus treasury investments
findings.detail: Over the past year the council held treasury investments between £20.7m and £75m. The balance sheet forecast shows this ends: from 31 March 2027 onwards the council moves from using internal resources to requiring external borrowing. New borrowing requirement is forecast at £36.758m (2026-27), £34.621m (2027-28), and £30.629m (2028-29), driven by a capital programme that exceeds available balance sheet resources.
findings.matters: A council's shift from being cash-generative (using reserves) to requiring structural external borrowing signals that capital ambitions now outstrip internal resources, requiring sustained market access and placing the council in a more dependent position on debt capital markets and refinancing.
findings.figures: Treasury investment position forecast to shift from (£47.585m) surplus in 2024-25 to £36.758m borrowing requirement in 2026-27; balance sheet resources declining from £148.795m to £124.936m
findings.quote: The consequence of this is that the Council moves from a position whereby it will have a need to borrow from 26/27 circa £37m reducing to £34m by 28/29.

findings.headline: Rent collection risk flagged due to cost of living pressures, though Housing Benefit eligibility limits exposure
findings.detail: The risk register notes that "the on-going cost of living crisis resulting from higher than anticipated inflation levels could have a detrimental impact on collection rates as some tenants struggle to pay their bills." Most HRA tenants are on Housing Benefit or Universal Credit, which mitigates the risk, but the council acknowledges this is an emerging threat to be monitored.
findings.matters: For an HRA already running deficits, any deterioration in rent collection would directly reduce income and accelerate reserve drawdown. While hedged by benefit coverage, this is a material tail risk.
findings.figures: Majority of HRA tenants in receipt of Housing Benefit or Universal Credit
findings.quote: The on-going cost of living crisis resulting from higher than anticipated inflation levels could have a detrimental impact on collection rates as some tenants struggle to pay their bills.

findings.headline: HRA capital investment severely constrained: only £2.990m budgeted for 2026/27, zero planned thereafter
findings.detail: The entire five-year capital plan consists of a one-off contribution of £2.990m toward Town Centre housing in 2026/27. Strategic forecasts for 2027/28–2030/31 show zero Revenue Contribution to Capital Outlay (RCCO). With 2,079 properties in stock and two large PFI contracts ending in 2036, this leaves almost no headroom to invest in housing maintenance, improvement, or expansion.
findings.matters: For a council managing 2,079 social housing units, the near-zero capital investment signals the HRA cannot fund maintenance or growth and will be dependent on external financing or reduced service levels as PFI contracts mature.
findings.figures: £2.990m RCCO in 2026/27; £0 in each of 2027/28–2030/31; total housing stock 2,079 units
findings.quote: The only requirement for HRA capital during the period covered by this report is a contribution of £2.990m toward the cost of additional housing in the Town Centre.

findings.headline: HRA is forecast to run annual deficits every year 2026/27 to 2030/31, with expenditure consistently exceeding income
findings.detail: Every year in the forecast shows a deficit: £3.438m (2026/27), £507k (2027/28), £609k (2028/29), £709k (2029/30), £557k (2030/31). This means the HRA is not operationally self-sufficient and must draw reserves to meet its annual costs. This is the mechanism driving the reserve depletion.
findings.matters: A self-financing account should not run persistent deficits. Annual deficits indicate the council's housing rents and charges are not sufficient to cover housing service costs, signalling underlying affordability or cost control problems.
findings.figures: 2026/27 deficit £3.438m; 2027-31 deficits £507k–£709k annually

findings.headline: Rent increases below the government maximum in 2022/23 and 2023/24 have reduced HRA capacity to fund capital investment
findings.detail: The council chose not to apply the full CPI+1% rent increases available in those years. This political decision is now constraining the HRA. The paper states this directly: "The ability of the HRA to support major capital projects has been diminished by the rent increases applied in 2022/23 and 2023/24 being below the maximum level." The multi-year impact compounds the reserve drain.
findings.matters: This shows the HRA's financial stress is partly a choice, not just market-driven. It signals political constraints on future rent-setting and illustrates that the council previously chose affordability over financial sustainability—a tension that may recur.
findings.figures: Maximum allowed CPI+1%; actual increases in 2022/23 and 2023/24 were below this; 2026/27 rate is 4.8% (CPI+1% at Sept 2025 CPI of 3.8%)
findings.quote: The ability of the HRA to support major capital projects has been diminished by the rent increases applied in 2022/23 and 2023/24 being below the maximum level (the Government Guidance of a maximum of CPI + 1%)

findings.headline: Two major PFI contracts covering 2,038 properties expire in 2036 with future maintenance arrangements and costs still unmodelled
findings.detail: PFI2 (1,429 sheltered housing dwellings) ends September 2036; PFI4 (609 properties) ends October 2036. The paper explicitly states the council has not yet determined what will happen post-expiry. When the contracts end, the council assumes direct responsibility for all repairs, maintenance, and building management of these 2,038 properties.
findings.matters: This is a major contingent liability. The current PFI arrangements hold maintenance obligations and costs that will shift entirely to the council in 10 years. Without a plan, there is a risk of unfunded service obligations or forced capital spending.
findings.figures: PFI2: 1,429 properties, £105m original construction value; PFI4: 609 properties, £77m original construction value; contracts end 2036
findings.quote: Thought will soon need to be given as to the arrangements for the stock currently managed as part of the PFI contracts, so that the financial impact on the HRA can be assessed more accurately.

findings.headline: HRA balances forecast to decline by £6.545m (30%) from 2025/26 to 2030/31, reducing financial buffer
findings.detail: Reserves drop from £22.173m to £15.628m. While still above the £3m minimum, the trajectory shows the HRA running annual deficits and drawing reserves every year. By 2030/31 the buffer is only about 5x the agreed minimum.
findings.matters: Declining reserves indicate the HRA is financially stressed and losing headroom to absorb shocks or invest. For a lender, this signals increasing financial vulnerability over the next five years.
findings.figures: £22.173m (start 2025/26) → £15.628m (end 2030/31); minimum required balance £3m
findings.quote: The financial projections for the HRA over the period 2025/26 to 2030/31 show an overall reduction in the level of balances from £22.173m at the start of 2025/26 to £15.628m at the end of 2030/31.

findings.headline: External auditors have made clear that funding day-to-day spending from reserves is a major risk requiring immediate remediation
findings.detail: The document repeatedly references the external auditors' concern that 'continuing to fund day to day spending through use of reserves is a major risk'. The opposition notes this is 'already of significant concern' when assessing the Administration budget and that reserves have fallen to levels described as 'critical'.
findings.matters: An auditor flagging reserve depletion as a major risk is a material warning. Councils using reserves to balance revenue budgets cannot sustain borrowing — repayment depends on surplus revenue generation, not reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Reserves described as at 'critical levels'
findings.quote: The Council's external auditors have made it clear that continuing to fund day to day spending through use of reserves is a major risk.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs driving £3m capital borrowing decision over 25 years
findings.detail: The Liberal Democrats propose £3m in prudential borrowing (25-year term) specifically to create temporary accommodation capacity and reduce reliance on expensive hotel and B&B provision. This is framed as a 'critical' priority due to 'recent trend in temporary accommodation'. The repayment of approximately £0.231m annually will commence 2028/29 and be the 'first call' against revenue savings generated from reduced hotel/B&B spend.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is identified as a critical budget pressure. A council taking on £3m capital debt to solve what is essentially a revenue problem signals unsustainable expenditure pressures. The capital-to-revenue arbitrage may not deliver sufficient savings to cover borrowing costs if demand continues to rise.
findings.figures: £3m prudential borrowing over 25 years; annual repayment ~£0.231m commencing 2028/29; current reliance on hotels and B&Bs cited as 'substantial pressures on the revenue side'
findings.quote: The proposal will be utilising capital investment to create revenue savings which the Liberal Democrats see as a main priority for the Capital Strategy. Given the recent trend in temporary accommodation the Liberal Democrats see this as essential and urgently required to reduce expenditure in this area.

findings.headline: Administration's £18.3m multi-year savings plan rated Amber with acknowledged high delivery risk and capability gaps
findings.detail: The report states the Administration is targeting £18.3m of savings through a cross-departmental multi-year plan. The document explicitly rates this as 'Amber' on its risk matrix and states: 'An honest assessment is that, in the current state, the deliverability risk is high. The Council does not yet consistently have the embedded capability, capacity or delivery infrastructure required to implement this scale of change at pace.' No benefits realisation framework has yet been established.
findings.matters: Large-scale undelivered savings programmes create fiscal instability. The council's own candid admission of capability and infrastructure gaps, combined with the track record of delivery failure, makes these savings highly uncertain. This directly threatens financial sustainability and debt repayment capacity.
findings.figures: £18.3m savings target across multi-year plan; recurring investment of '£2-3m recurrent' with no detailed year-by-year breakdown
findings.quote: An honest assessment is that, in the current state, the deliverability risk is high. The Council does not yet consistently have the embedded capability, capacity or delivery infrastructure required to implement this scale of change at pace.

findings.headline: Council has repeatedly failed to deliver budgeted savings, driving reserves to critical levels
findings.detail: The opposition document states the council has had 'a consistent pattern of overspending' across three years, particularly in Children's and Adult Social Care and homelessness. Multiple years of substantial savings proposals have 'failed to be delivered', resulting in reserves being drawn down to critical levels. External auditors have flagged 'continuing to fund day to day spending through use of reserves is a major risk'.
findings.matters: A pattern of savings not being delivered is a fundamental fiscal risk signal; it indicates management capability issues and unsustainability of the current financial position. Lenders depend on councils delivering promised savings to meet debt obligations.
findings.figures: 2025/26 budget reductions totalling £3.164m were 'judged to be unachievable'; only £1.369m now estimated achievable in 2026/27
findings.quote: Following multiple years in which the Administration has proposed substantial savings in order to meet that balanced budget, which it has failed to deliver, combined with successive years of overspending, in particular through Children's Social Care, Adult Social Care and homelessness, the Council is in our view, at a crisis point. A similar failure to achieve the savings proposed in the Administration budget would see reserves fall below critical levels.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficit of £0.357m to be recovered from 2026-27, driven by below-forecast new properties
findings.detail: The Council's 2025-26 forecast Council Tax base of 59,501 was not achieved; actual is 59,411 due to fewer new properties being added than expected. This shortfall drives a Collection Fund deficit of £0.357m (Council share £0.299m) to be recovered in 2026-27.
findings.matters: Slower property growth than forecast indicates softer economic activity in the borough; this deficit must be absorbed from 2026-27 resources
findings.figures: Collection Fund deficit £0.357m (£0.299m council share); tax base shortfall of 90 properties
findings.quote: The number of new properties being added to the Council Tax base has been less than forecast during this financial year, meaning the actual value is currently 59,411.

findings.headline: General reserves forecast to remain above policy minimum, but heavily committed to future capital and reform funding
findings.detail: Projected closing reserves at end 2025-26 are £49.023m (down £3.616m from opening), above the £36m minimum. However, reserves are committed to: £1.432m for Bus Reform (2027-28), Joint Fund reserves for NHS integration, and regeneration reserves for capital projects. The general fund balance is not to be reduced below £18.865m.
findings.matters: While headline reserves appear adequate, committed allocations to specific programmes mean available reserves for general contingency are lower than stated totals; this limits flexibility for unexpected pressures
findings.figures: £49.023m closing reserves forecast 2025-26; £36m policy minimum; £18.865m general fund balance; £1.432m committed to Bus Reform 2027-28
findings.quote: A number of these reserves are committed to finance expenditure planned for future financial years meaning they are not available for alternative use. This includes: a further £1.432m for Bus Reform required in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Transformation programme savings of £2.000m depends on external procurement not yet commissioned
findings.detail: The council commissioned an external strategic partner for discovery work on transformation savings in Adults Social Care, Children's Services and Housing, identifying 'significant transformation savings over a period of four years'. To deliver £2.000m in 2026-27, the council 'will now need to begin the procurement process'. Savings are undelivered and procurement has not started.
findings.matters: £2.000m (10% of the gap-bridging plan) depends on external procurement and delivery that has not yet begun; this is a material delivery risk to budget balance
findings.figures: £2.000m transformation savings required for 2026-27; savings identified but procurement not yet started
findings.quote: To move to the delivery stage the Council will now need to begin the procurement process to support the delivery of the savings set out in this report.

findings.headline: New £5.459m permanent investment in Children's Services following failed improvement returns
findings.detail: Investment made to drive Children's Services improvements was expected to generate returns through service improvements and demand reduction. However, increasing demand and care-sector complexity have prevented realisation of those returns. The temporary investment is now being made permanent.
findings.matters: This signals that demand and complexity pressures are outpacing the council's ability to drive efficiency gains; transformation assumptions may be optimistic
findings.figures: £5.459m permanent investment required for 2026-27
findings.quote: This investment was funded through expected returns realised as improvements across the service were made. At the same time, the demand and complexity of need, coupled with sufficiency across the care sector has impacted on the ability to generate the returns on this investment.

findings.headline: £3.164m of undelivered savings from 2025-26 being rolled forward as base budget pressure
findings.detail: As of December 2025, only 80% of approved 2025-26 budget reductions have been delivered. The remaining 20% rated Red or Amber (at-risk) amount to £3.164m. This undelivered saving is being added back as a permanent base budget requirement for 2026-27, indicating recurrent delivery challenges.
findings.matters: Previous years' savings failures becoming permanent budget pressures suggests the council has difficulty achieving its planned reduction targets in-year
findings.figures: £3.164m of 2025-26 budget reductions not delivered; 20% of approved savings in Red/Amber status
findings.quote: Non-delivery will have an adverse effect on the 2026/27 base budget. Therefore, £3.164m of base budget provision has been included within the Council's revenue budget for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Children's Services income pressure of £2.421m: Health has ended financial contributions to placements from January 2026
findings.detail: From January 2026, Health will no longer contribute financially to Social Care placements for Children Looked After (except in specific CHC-funded cases). The council previously budgeted for this health income but it is now unachievable, requiring removal of £2.421m from income budget and addition to expenditure base.
findings.matters: This represents a structural change in the joint funding model for looked-after children, shifting cost entirely to the council with no notice period for budget adjustment
findings.figures: £2.421m income budget pressure in 2026-27
findings.quote: From January 2026, the Council will have nil financial contributions towards Social Care placements from Health for the current cohort of Children Looked After. (This could vary for any new children who meet CHC funding criteria, or alternatively any existing children whose circumstances change). As a result, the income budget held within this area becomes unachievable and needs to be removed from the base budget.

findings.headline: Foundation Living Wage commitment creates £5.352m uncontrollable cost pressure for 2026-27
findings.detail: The council pays care providers the Foundation Living Wage (£13.45/hour from 1 May 2026) rather than National Minimum Wage, an increase of 6.7% from the previous rate of £12.60. This requires an additional £5.352m budget provision for 2026-27 alone. This is a policy commitment that cannot be reduced mid-year.
findings.matters: This is a committed cost increase with no service scope flexibility; it demonstrates the council is subject to price inflation on essential statutory services it cannot avoid or defer
findings.figures: £5.352m additional budget requirement for 2026-27; wage rate increase from £12.60 to £13.45 per hour (6.7%)
findings.quote: The Foundation Living Wage will increase from 1 May 2026 going from a rate of £12.60 to £13.45 per hour, an increase of 6.7%. The additional budgetary provision required for this rate increase is £5.352m for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Schools DSG deficit escalating dramatically to £32.919m by 2026-27
findings.detail: The dedicated schools grant (DSG) account is forecast to move to a deficit of £9.753m by end of 2025-26, worsening to a cumulative £32.919m by 2026-27. The main driver is the High Needs Block: the Government has 'cash limited' high needs funding for 2026-27 rather than using the national funding formula, while demand for special schools and out-of-borough placements continues to rise. This is held off-balance-sheet under statutory override until 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: The growing DSG deficit indicates structural demand pressures the council cannot control within its funded allocation, and the 31 March 2028 override deadline means this will hit the balance sheet as a liabilities crisis if not resolved
findings.figures: £9.753m deficit forecast end 2025-26; £32.919m cumulative deficit by 2026-27
findings.quote: the financial position of the DSG has worsened with increasing cumulative deficits now being forecast for 2025/26 (£9.753m) and 2026/27 (£32.919m)

findings.headline: Current year (2025-26) forecasts £15.199m adverse variance despite management action
findings.detail: At Quarter 3 Month 9, the Council is forecasting a £15.199m overspend against a budget of £325.486m. This has improved from Quarter 2 by £5.894m through management actions, but remains substantial. The three main pressure areas are Adult Social Care (£8.996m), Children's Services (£5.407m), and Place (£4.563m). Any underfunded outturn will require use of general reserves.
findings.matters: A significant overspend in 2025-26 will reduce reserves available to support the 2026-27 budget and impacts the council's financial resilience going forward
findings.figures: £15.199m Q3 forecast variance; Adult Social Care £8.996m, Children's Services £5.407m, Place £4.563m
findings.quote: there still remains a significant projected budget overspend which will impact on the size of the budget gap in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy for 2026/27 and future years and the level of Earmarked Reserves.

findings.headline: Place Directorate (primarily town centre property portfolio) under £4.169m pressure from reduced rents, void costs, and backdated Business Rates liability
findings.detail: The Growth Division is forecasting £4.169m adverse variance, almost entirely from the Town Centre Property portfolio. Pressures include reduced rent agreements being sought by tenants, increased Spindles Shopping Centre voids and service charge payable, and Business Rates for Spindles Office space backdated to May 2024, creating an unexpected 'forecast far exceeding initial budget expectations.' This signals weakness in local economic conditions and portfolio management issues.
findings.matters: Council property portfolio performance is a bellwether of local economic conditions; unexpected liabilities (like backdated rates) represent uncontrolled risks; voids and rent reductions signal tenant distress
findings.figures: £4.169m Growth Division adverse variance; £4.563m total Place variance; £2.064m Town Centre pressure highlighted
findings.quote: The main reason behind the forecast budget pressure within this area relates to Town Centre Property portfolio. This pressure relates to reductions in rent as reduced rent agreements are currently being sought by both prospective and sitting tenants. In addition, rent agreements currently being proposed, regularly include service charge caps or service charge costs that are included within a cumulative rent figure. An increased Council footprint and voids within the Spindles Shopping Centre have also led to increased service charge payable and foregone rent.

findings.headline: Capital programme slashed by £52.048m mid-year (from £122.248m to £70.200m), suggesting poor project planning or external blockers to delivery
findings.detail: Following the 'Annual Review,' the 2025/26 capital programme was reduced by 43%. Capital spend to 31 December is £40.189m (57.25% of forecast), lower than the prior-year profile of 61.23% at the same point. The magnitude of the mid-year reduction and slower spend profile suggests either significant project delays or reforecasting errors in the original budget.
findings.matters: Large mid-year capital reductions can signal project delays, planning failures, or external constraints (land acquisition, planning delays); this impacts regeneration delivery and economic strategy
findings.figures: £52.048m reduction; £70.200m revised vs £122.248m Month 6 position; £40.189m spend to date (57.25% of forecast); prior-year profile 61.23%
findings.quote: This leaves the revised 2025/26 Capital Programme at £70.200m compared with the Month 6 position presented to Cabinet of £122.248m, an in year reduction of £52.048m

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast at £9.753m for 2025/26, with £23.166m in-year deficit projected for 2026/27 and cumulative position of £32.919m by end of 2026/27
findings.detail: The DSG is in severe deficit driven primarily by High Needs Block pressures (£9.233m overspend). Government announced on 17 December 2025 that the national high needs funding formula will be paused, with funding frozen at 2025/26 allocations—negatively impacting the 2026/27 forecast further. While the statutory override currently excludes this from the council's reserve position, government has indicated intent to transfer SEND costs to Whitehall from 2028/29, after which this deficit could fall back on the council.
findings.matters: A £32.9m cumulative DSG deficit trajectory is unsustainable; the statutory override ends in 2027/28, after which this could become a council liability; even before then, it signals major structural pressures in special education provision
findings.figures: £9.753m 2025/26 year-end forecast; £23.166m 2026/27 forecast; £32.919m cumulative by 31 March 2027; £9.233m High Needs Block overspend
findings.quote: The initial 2026/27 forecast is for an in-year deficit of £23.166m, driven mainly by continued pressures within the High Needs Block together with the impact of alignment to the 2026/26 budget setting process and the reduced High Needs Block funding announced by the Government on 17 December 2025

findings.headline: 16% of approved 2025/26 budget savings (£4.221m) rated as high-risk and unlikely to be delivered, compounding medium-term budget gap
findings.detail: Of £26.584m approved savings, only 80% are green-rated (on track). 4% (£1.059m) are amber (at-risk but potentially achievable), and 16% (£4.221m) are red-rated with high risk of non-achievement. These non-deliveries include the Children's Investment Plan (£2.116m), Adult Social Care initiatives (£1.373m), and Place service review (£0.545m). The paper states: 'given the overall financial pressures facing the Council, the uncertainty around the deliverability of the remaining 16% of savings is of concern.
